title: Does Group Fairness Guarantee Recourse Fairness? An Empirical Test Across Two Decision Domains
content: Automated decision systems are commonly audited with group fairness metrics such as demographic parity and equalized odds, which compare outcome or error rates across protected groups. Algorithmic recourse asks a different question: for a person who receives an unfavourable decision, how large a change would be needed to obtain a favourable one? We measure how two standard bias mitigation methods, Reweighing and a covariance-penalized logistic regression, change the recourse gap between groups, using linear classifiers whose distance to the decision boundary has an exact closed form. Experiments use Adult Census Income (sex) and COMPAS recidivism data (race), with Mann–Whitney U tests and rank-biserial effect sizes over 30 random train/test splits, plus two robustness checks: removing the protected attribute from the model inputs, and sweeping the penalty strength. On Adult, the two methods achieved similar group-fairness scores (mean SPD −0.087 versus −0.094; AOD 0.068 versus 0.057) but different recourse disparities (rank-biserial r = 0.205 versus −0.083), and the difference persisted on the same denied individuals. After the penalty, the privileged-minus-unprivileged distance gap was negative at the 10th and 25th percentiles (−0.126, −0.160) and positive from the median upward (+0.083 at the median, +0.725 at the 90th percentile): denied men had the longer upper tail. With sex removed, Reweighing’s r moved only from 0.311 to 0.293 and the penalty’s sign change disappeared (r = 0.040). COMPAS was an exploratory secondary evaluation: λ was selected on the reported split, and small denied-group samples limited power to detect modest disparities. The similar SPD and AOD values are observed properties of these fitted models, not an enforced match, and do not rank the methods in general. Similar outcome-based fairness scores do not establish similar geometric recourse burdens, and geometric distance alone does not establish feasible real-world recourse; the results support reporting recourse disparities and their distributions alongside conventional group-fairness metrics.
